date_convention: BCE pairs are older to younger; null means no absolute range justified here. Broad phase brackets are display context, not direct dates of every object.
independence_note: Groups identify a principal lineage; HARP sources share field observations. Soil, lipid and plant measurements differ but share LWS sites, context chronology and excavation selection. No vote count or pooled significance is calculated.

evidence.title: Excavations at Harappa 1994-1995: New Perspectives on the Indus Script, Craft Activities, and City Organization
evidence.observation: The excavators distinguish widely shared urban traits from older, locally diverse farming and pastoral traditions.
evidence.interpretation: A definition based on urban traits will stop recognizing some continuing local activity when those traits disappear.
evidence.chronology: Early through Late Harappan regional framework
evidence.confidence: high for the stated scholarly argument; not a measured rate

independence.note: HARP Harappa excavation and regional interpretation

evidence.title: Fifty-Five Years of Archaeological Research in Pakistan: The Prehistoric Periods
evidence.locator: Printed pp.202–203; PDF p.7, Table10.2 and Late Harappan paragraph
evidence.observation: The excavators describe regional exchange and craft activity at Harappa in Cemetery H levels, approximately 1800 to perhaps 1500 BCE, alongside loss of script and standardized weights.
evidence.interpretation: Local posturban activity is visible even where particular administrative markers cease. The prose and provisional phase table have different end-date uncertainty.
evidence.chronology: Late Harappan/Cemetery H, source prose c.1800–1500 BCE
evidence.confidence: moderate to high for site activity; final calendar limit provisional

independence.note: HARP Harappa excavation and research synthesis

evidence.title: Measuring the Harappan world: Insights into the Indus order and cosmology
evidence.observation: The chapter reports loss of cubical stone weights after the urban period and a related system in Early Historic South Asia, while calling the intervening relationship unresolved.
evidence.interpretation: Later recurrence requires a dated transmission sequence. It cannot fill the intervening centuries; Dholavira supplies a regional exception to the broad disappearance statement.
evidence.chronology: Urban end c.1900 BCE; Early Historic comparison c.600 BCE
evidence.confidence: high for the source statement; direct transmission unestablished

independence.note: HARP Harappa weight measurements and broader comparative synthesis

evidence.title: Chanhu-Daro Excavations 1935-36
evidence.locator: Printed p.143; PDF p.164, seals and amulets discussion
evidence.observation: Most Jhukar seals or amulets described here are round. The excavator records no clear script on them, while allowing ambiguous marks.
evidence.interpretation: The familiar inscribed square seal ceases to be the only relevant search target. This absence cannot establish whether writing continued on an unpreserved medium.
evidence.chronology: Jhukar is stratigraphically post-Harappan here; no modern absolute date inferred from this legacy report
evidence.confidence: high for the inspected assemblage; relative chronology only
scenario_implications: administrative material changed; medium-switch remains untested

evidence.title: Chanhu-Daro Excavations 1935-36
evidence.observation: The report describes extensive brick removal in upper Mound II and disturbed contexts containing older objects.
evidence.interpretation: An urban-period object in a later layer can be residual or reused. Such a find needs a depositional assessment before counting as continued manufacture.
evidence.chronology: Successive Harappan and Jhukar occupations; relative chronology
evidence.confidence: high for reported disturbance; specific reuse is an excavator inference

evidence.title: Excavations at Dholavira (1989–90 to 2004–2005)
evidence.locator: Section5.6; printed p.103, PDF p.120; chronology p.104
evidence.observation: Stage VI follows a short desertion and occupies a reduced area. Rectangular inscribed seals and cubical chert weights persist, alongside changed pottery and housing.
evidence.interpretation: The report describes marker persistence into a reduced settlement, challenging a single conventional cutoff. Its phase envelope spans 1900 BCE; primary contexts and absolute dates are needed to establish post-1900 last use and exclude residual objects.
evidence.chronology: Preliminary Stage VI assignment c.1950–1800 BCE
evidence.confidence: high for report description; moderate for provisional absolute placement
scenario_implications: supports phased regionalization and local interruption

evidence.title: Excavations at Dholavira (1989–90 to 2004–2005)
evidence.locator: Section5.7 and chronology; printed p.104, PDF p.121
evidence.observation: Stage VII follows a longer, unquantified desertion and contains circular houses with urban attributes absent. Its provisional range is c.1500–1450 BCE.
evidence.interpretation: Return to the same site can follow a real break. Similarity to current regional houses cannot establish occupation through the intervening centuries.
evidence.chronology: Preliminary Stage VII assignment c.1500–1450 BCE
evidence.confidence: high for the reported gap and forms; moderate for calendar range

evidence.title: Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization
evidence.locator: Settlement Dynamics in the Harappan Domain, Sindh preservation paragraph
evidence.observation: The primary landform study distinguishes well-preserved upper Sindh sites from southwestern alluvial areas where later sediment could cover former settlements.
evidence.interpretation: Burial is a geographically specific mechanism. The statement predicts where surface surveys can miss deposits; it does not count hidden settlements.
evidence.chronology: Holocene landform sequence, including Harappan occupation
evidence.confidence: high for mapped landform contrast; individual buried-site presence untested

independence.note: Primary geomorphology plus previously compiled settlement distributions

scenario_implications: supports differentiated detectability, not universal burial

evidence.title: Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization

evidence.interpretation: Regional loss and redistribution can coexist. This synthesis is not an independent excavation count or a demonstrated migration route.

evidence.title: Landscapes of Urbanization and De-Urbanization: A Large-Scale Approach to Investigating the Indus Civilization’s Settlement Distributions in Northwest India
evidence.locator: XML S005 Discussion and S006 Conclusions
evidence.observation: Integrated surveys show different local settlement trajectories. The authors identify possible northeastern reoccupation but require renewed coverage to separate it from earlier survey practices.
evidence.interpretation: Mapped site density is not a direct census of people. Apparent relocation must survive a common survey frame and reliable phase assignments.
evidence.chronology: Early, Mature, Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware survey categories
evidence.confidence: high for documented survey qualifications; movement of particular people untested

independence.note: Integrated northwest India surveys, including Land, Water and Settlement fieldwork

scenario_implications: distribution change supported; simple eastward arrows premature

evidence.title: Geoarchaeological insights into the location of Indus settlements on the plains of northwest India
evidence.observation: Soil profiles recover former surfaces and low levee or dune settings now obscured by later modification. Masudpur profiles include buried horizons below the current surface.
evidence.interpretation: A flat modern field can conceal earlier landscape structure. Buried soil alone does not establish a settlement or its date.
evidence.chronology: Holocene geomorphology associated with named Indus sites; individual profile dates retained in the source
evidence.confidence: high for sampled profiles; coverage outside profiles unmeasured

independence.note: Land, Water and Settlement, four excavated sites and their surrounding soil profiles

scenario_implications: supports sub-surface sampling before negative conclusions

evidence.title: Lipid residues in pottery from the Indus Civilisation in northwest India
evidence.observation: The study analyzed 172 sherds from seven sites. Its small urban/posturban comparisons at Alamgirpur and Masudpur VII found no statistically detected shift in the reported lipid isotope variables.
evidence.interpretation: Domestic practices can remain archaeologically measurable across changing material categories. Limited samples and mixed product signatures prevent an equivalence claim.
evidence.chronology: Mature Harappan c.2600/2500–1900 BCE and Late Harappan c.1900–1300 BCE; samples assigned by context
evidence.confidence: high for the published analytical result; moderate for culinary continuity

independence.note: Seven sites; urban/posturban comparison principally Alamgirpur and Masudpur VII; partly shares Land, Water and Settlement excavations

evidence.title: ‘Multi-cropping’, Intercropping and Adaptation to Variable Environments in Indus South Asia
evidence.locator: Supplement TableS23; accepted PDF pp.91–92; prior crop audit run-v2
evidence.observation: Bahola retains winter and summer crop categories in Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware assemblages. The published winter share rises from 6.87% to 17.29%.
evidence.interpretation: Repertoire retention can accompany changing proportions. Pooled plant-remain percentages do not establish unchanged fields, diets or social institutions.
evidence.chronology: Source-assigned Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware phases
evidence.confidence: high for published phase summaries; local management continuity unmeasured

independence.note: Land, Water and Settlement excavation samples and Bates thesis; same crop observations audited on 25 October

scenario_implications: selective retention with adaptation; prior audited evidence

evidence.title: ‘Multi-cropping’, Intercropping and Adaptation to Variable Environments in Indus South Asia
evidence.locator: Burj site sequence discussion and supplementary TablesS8–S9
evidence.observation: Burj has Early Harappan and Painted Grey Ware plant assemblages separated by an occupation break.
evidence.interpretation: Repeated use of a location is compatible with a hiatus. This site is a required counterexample when designing a continuity sample.
evidence.chronology: Early Harappan to later Painted Grey Ware; no continuous intervening sequence
evidence.confidence: high for reported sequence; exact break duration not estimated here

independence.note: Land, Water and Settlement excavation samples and Bates thesis; same crop observations audited on 25 October

evidence.title: Recent Excavations at Alamgirpur, Meerut District: A Preliminary Report
evidence.observation: Alamgirpur’s excavators report no clear stratigraphic break and possible pottery overlap, while noting a protracted gap in available AMS dates and seven failed dating submissions.
evidence.interpretation: Stratigraphic proximity and calendar continuity remain distinct. The dating conflict is unresolved and the transition needs new directly associated samples.
evidence.chronology: Harappan-to-Painted Grey Ware transition; precise bridge unresolved
evidence.confidence: high for report’s stated conflict; uninterrupted occupation unresolved

independence.note: BHU Alamgirpur 2008 excavations; overlaps later soil, lipid and plant publications

scenario_implications: a strong test case requiring chronology repair

evidence.title: Archaeobotanical data from a Baran settlement (4,300–3,400 yrs bp) in the Ghaggar basin (northwestern India) reveals continuity of the Indus crop package after the Meghalayan stage drought
evidence.locator: Primary chronology, source PDF p.7; prior audit REPORT and run-v2
evidence.observation: The Jognakhera paper reports green gram at 1880–1691 cal BCE and rice at 1517–1428 cal BCE.
evidence.interpretation: Dated posturban crops supply intermediate activity. The sampled deposits still need a complete phase join before assigning them to a named later pottery culture.

evidence.confidence: moderate; source supplement and full sample-date ledger remain unavailable
